This edition has real terminals in it

Every "Live sandbox" box below is a small bash simulator running entirely in your browser — a real (if simplified) shell with its own filesystem, seeded with the exact same practice data as Appendix B's setup script. Type commands, press Enter, and see real output. It supports pipes, redirects, globs, grep/sed/awk, permissions, background jobs, and for/if/while loops.

Getting Out of Your Shell

The 20% of bash that does 80% of the work.

12 chapters12 labsAnswer keyCheat sheet

A short, practical book for people who have opened a terminal, felt vaguely uneasy, and closed it again. By the end you will move around a Linux system with confidence, chain commands together, edit text without opening an editor, manage processes and permissions, and write scripts that other people can read.

How to Use This Book

Every chapter follows the same shape: a short explanation, commands you can actually type, a lab that gives you something concrete to do, and a handful of questions whose answers are hidden until you click them. Do the labs. Reading about the shell is like reading about swimming.

You need a Linux or macOS terminal, or WSL on Windows. Check that you are running bash:

$ echo $SHELL
/bin/bash
$ bash --version
GNU bash, version 5.2.21(1)-release

If it says zsh (the default on modern macOS), almost everything here still works — zsh is bash-compatible for the 80% this book covers. Where it matters, the text says so. To follow along in real bash on a Mac, just type bash to start one.

Set up your sandbox first

Every lab runs inside one throwaway directory so you can experiment without fear. Appendix B contains a setup script that builds it — copy that script into a file called setup.sh, then run:

$ bash setup.sh
Sandbox ready at: /home/dave/shell-lab
$ cd ~/shell-lab

Do this before Lab 1. To start over at any point, rm -rf ~/shell-lab and run it again.

Conventions

A line beginning with $ is something you type; the $ is the prompt and is not part of the command. Lines without it are output. Text in ANGLE_BRACKETS or written as FILE is a placeholder you replace with a real value.

Chapter 1The Shell in Ten Minutes

The shell is a program that reads what you type, runs it, and prints the result. That is the whole idea. When you open a terminal you get a shell — usually bash — sitting in a loop, waiting.

What makes it worth learning is not any single command. It is that every command is a small tool that reads text and writes text, and the shell lets you connect them. Once you internalize that, a hundred commands become a combinatorial toolkit instead of a hundred things to memorize.

Reading the prompt

A typical prompt looks like this:

dave@web-01:~/projects/api$

Four pieces of information: your username, the machine you are on, the directory you are in (~ means your home directory), and a $ meaning you are an ordinary user. A # instead of $ means you are root — pay attention when you see it.

Anatomy of a command

$ ls -l --color=auto /var/log
  │   │       │          │
  │   │       │          └─ argument: what to operate on
  │   │       └─ long option with a value
  │   └─ short option (flags can bundle: -la is -l -a)
  └─ the command

Three rules cover nearly all syntax you will meet:

  • Whitespace separates arguments. rm my file.txt deletes two files, not one. Quote names with spaces: rm "my file.txt".
  • Short options are single letters with one dash and can be combined: ls -l -a -h equals ls -lah. Long options use two dashes and are not combinable: --human-readable.
  • Order usually does not matter for options, but arguments are positional: cp SOURCE DEST is not the same as cp DEST SOURCE.

The first six commands

$ pwd              # where am I?
/home/dave
$ ls               # what is here?
Documents  Downloads  projects  notes.txt
$ cd projects      # go somewhere
$ whoami           # who am I logged in as?
dave
$ date             # what time is it (on this machine)?
Fri Aug 14 09:12:44 PDT 2026
$ clear            # wipe the screen (Ctrl-L does the same)

Getting help without leaving the terminal

You will not remember every flag, and you are not supposed to. Learn the three ways to look things up instead.

CommandWhat it gives you
man lsThe full manual page. Press / to search, n for next match, q to quit.
ls --helpA one-screen summary. Faster than man for "what was that flag again?"
help cdFor shell builtins like cd, export, if — these have no man page of their own.
type lsTells you whether something is a builtin, an alias, a function, or a program on disk.
apropos compressSearches man page descriptions when you don't know the command's name.
$ type cd
cd is a shell builtin
$ type ls
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
$ type -a python3
python3 is /usr/bin/python3
Tip

man pages are dense but predictably organized: NAME, SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, OPTIONS, EXAMPLES. Many people jump straight to the bottom — G in the pager — because the EXAMPLES section is often all you need.

Four keys that pay for themselves today

  • Tab — completes commands, filenames, and paths. Press it constantly. Press it twice to see all matches. This is not a convenience feature; it is your defense against typos in destructive commands.
  • ↑ / ↓ — walk back through commands you already ran.
  • Ctrl-C — kill the command that is currently running. Use it when something hangs.
  • Ctrl-D — end of input. On an empty prompt it logs you out of the shell.
Careful

The shell has no undo and no recycle bin. rm means gone. The habit that saves you: type the command with ls first, look at what it matches, then change ls to rm by pressing ↑ and editing. Chapter 3 goes deeper.

Lab 1 · Orientation
  1. Open a terminal. Print your current directory, your username, and the machine's name (hostname).
  2. Find out whether echo is a builtin or a program on disk.
  3. Use ls --help to find the flag that sorts files by modification time, then run it on your home directory.
  4. Open the manual for date, search inside it for the string %Y, and use what you find to print today's date as 2026-08-14.
  5. Type sleep 60, then get your prompt back without waiting a minute.

Questions

What is the difference between a shell builtin and a regular command?

A builtin is implemented inside bash itself (cd, export, echo, test); a regular command is a separate executable file the shell finds and runs (ls at /usr/bin/ls). It matters for two reasons: builtins have no man page (use help), and only builtins can change the shell's own state — which is why cd must be a builtin. An external program could never change your shell's current directory.

Why does ls -lah work but ls --human-readable-all not?

Single-dash short options are single characters, so bash-era tools let you bundle them: -lah is parsed as three separate flags. Double-dash long options are whole words and each needs its own --: ls --human-readable --all.

You typed a long command and it is hanging. What do you press, and what if that does not work?

Ctrl-C sends the interrupt signal (SIGINT) and stops most programs. If the program ignores it, Ctrl-Z suspends it and gives you your prompt back, after which you can kill it (Chapter 9). If your terminal itself is garbled rather than hung, reset repairs it.

What does ~ mean, and what is ~/projects?

~ expands to your home directory, typically /home/yourname (or /Users/yourname on macOS). So ~/projects is /home/dave/projects. ~otheruser expands to that user's home directory. The expansion is done by the shell before the command ever sees it.

Chapter 2Moving Around

Linux organizes everything into one tree that starts at /, the root. There are no drive letters. A USB stick, a network share, and your hard disk all appear as directories somewhere under /.

Absolute and relative paths

An absolute path starts at the root and works everywhere: /var/log/syslog. A relative path starts from wherever you currently are: log/syslog. Four shorthands do most of the work:

SymbolMeans
.the current directory
..the parent directory
~your home directory
-(with cd) the directory you were in previously
$ cd /var/log        # absolute
$ cd ..              # up one level, now in /var
$ cd -               # back to /var/log
$ cd                 # with no argument: straight home
$ cd ../../etc       # relative, climbing two levels then down

Seeing what is there

$ ls                 # names only
$ ls -l              # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
$ ls -a              # include hidden files (names starting with .)
$ ls -lh             # sizes as 4.0K, 2.3M instead of raw bytes
$ ls -lt             # newest first
$ ls -ltr            # newest last — handy for logs, the interesting line ends up nearest your prompt
$ ls -ld /etc        # info about the directory itself, not its contents

Read a long listing left to right:

-rw-r--r--  1 dave  staff   1420 Aug 14 09:03 notes.txt
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘  │  │     │       │        │          │
│ │  │  │   │  │     │       │        │          └ name
│ │  │  │   │  │     │       │        └ last modified
│ │  │  │   │  │     │       └ size in bytes
│ │  │  │   │  │     └ group
│ │  │  │   │  └ owner
│ │  │  │   └ number of hard links
│ │  │  └ permissions for everyone else
│ │  └ permissions for the group
│ └ permissions for the owner
└ type: - file, d directory, l symlink

Chapter 8 unpacks the permission bits. For now: d at the start means directory, and l means symbolic link.

Globbing: patterns instead of names

The shell expands wildcards before running the command. ls *.txt never reaches ls as *.txt — bash replaces it with the list of matching filenames first. This is one of the most important facts in this book, and Chapter 10 returns to it.

PatternMatches
*any characters, including none — *.log, report*
?exactly one character — file?.txt matches file1.txt, not file10.txt
[abc]one character from the set — file[123].txt
[a-z]one character from the range
{a,b}brace expansion — file.{txt,md} becomes two words; unlike the others it works even if no file matches
$ ls *.log                     # every log file here
$ ls report_2026-0[1-6]*.csv   # first half of the year
$ mkdir -p project/{src,test,docs}   # creates three directories in one go
$ echo {1..5}
1 2 3 4 5
Careful

A glob is not a regular expression. In glob syntax * means "anything"; in regex it means "zero or more of the previous thing". grep *.txt and ls *.txt are doing entirely different things with that asterisk. Chapter 7 covers regex properly.

Seeing structure

$ tree -L 2            # directory tree, two levels deep (install if missing)
$ ls -R                 # recursive listing, the always-available fallback
$ du -sh *              # size of each item here, summarized
$ du -sh . | sort -h    # what is eating my disk
$ df -h                 # free space per filesystem

Directories worth knowing

PathContains
/home/youyour files. The only place you can write without permission games.
/etcsystem configuration, all plain text
/var/loglog files
/tmpscratch space, wiped on reboot, writable by everyone
/usr/bin, /binthe programs you run
/opthand-installed third-party software
/proca fake filesystem exposing kernel and process state as files

  3. Jump back to logs with a single two-character argument.

Questions

Why does cd with no arguments not throw an error?

Bare cd is defined to mean "go to $HOME". It is the fastest way home from anywhere. Likewise cd - toggles between the last two directories, which is excellent when you are bouncing between a config directory and a log directory.

ls *.txt prints "no such file or directory: *.txt". What happened?

No file matched the pattern, so bash left the literal string *.txt in place and passed it to ls, which then complained about a file with that odd name. This is standard (and slightly surprising) bash behavior. You can make unmatched globs expand to nothing instead with shopt -s nullglob, but knowing why the error looks like that is usually enough.

What is the difference between ls -l /etc and ls -ld /etc?

ls -l /etc lists the contents of the directory. ls -ld /etc lists the directory entry itself — one line showing /etc's own permissions, owner, and size. Use -d whenever you want to inspect a directory rather than look inside it.

You are in /home/dave/projects/api/src. Write the shortest way to get to /home/dave/projects/web.

cd ../../web — up out of src, up out of api, then down into web. cd ~/projects/web is the same length and arguably clearer; both are fine.

Why is ls -ltr a favorite of experienced admins?

-t sorts by time, -r reverses it, so the most recently modified file appears at the bottom of the output — right above your prompt, where your eyes already are. On a directory with hundreds of log files, that is the file you almost always want.

Chapter 3Creating, Copying, Destroying

Six commands cover essentially all file management: mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm, ln. They are simple. The care goes into not destroying things.

Creating

$ mkdir reports                 # one directory
$ mkdir -p a/b/c                # create parents as needed; no error if it exists
$ touch notes.txt               # create an empty file, or update its timestamp
$ touch f{1..3}.txt             # f1.txt f2.txt f3.txt

-p is worth a habit. It makes mkdir idempotent: running it twice is harmless, which is exactly what you want in a script.

Copying and moving

$ cp notes.txt notes.bak            # copy to a new name
$ cp notes.txt ~/backup/            # copy into a directory, keeping the name
$ cp -r project/ project-copy/      # -r for directories (recursive)
$ cp -a project/ project-copy/      # -a: recursive AND preserve times, owner, permissions
$ cp -i important.conf /etc/        # -i: prompt before overwriting
$ mv draft.txt final.txt            # rename
$ mv *.log logs/                    # move many files into a directory
$ mv -n a.txt b/                    # -n: never overwrite

mv is both "rename" and "move" — on the same filesystem it just rewrites a directory entry, which is why moving a 40 GB file within one disk is instant while copying it is not.

The trailing-slash trap

cp -r src dest behaves differently depending on whether dest already exists: if it does, you get dest/src; if it does not, src is copied to dest. When you care about the distinction, use rsync, whose rules are explicit: rsync -a src/ dest/ (with the trailing slash on the source) copies the contents.

Deleting, carefully

$ rm oldfile.txt
$ rm -r olddir/            # recursive: directory and everything inside
$ rm -f stubborn.txt       # force: no prompts, no error if missing
$ rmdir emptydir/          # only works if the directory is empty — a useful safety net

There is no trash can. rm unlinks the file and the space is reclaimed. Three habits that prevent almost every accident:

  1. Look before you delete. Run the pattern with ls first, then press ↑ and change ls to rm.
  2. Never type rm -rf with a variable or a glob you have not just inspected. rm -rf "$DIR"/* where $DIR is accidentally empty means rm -rf /*.
  3. Prefer rmdir when you expect empty. If it refuses, something is in there you did not know about.
$ ls old_reports_*.csv          # 1. inspect
old_reports_2024.csv  old_reports_2025.csv
$ rm old_reports_*.csv          # 2. same pattern, now with rm
Tip

Adding alias rm='rm -i' to your .bashrc is tempting but teaches you to reflexively hit y, which is worse. A better habit: put junk in /tmp so it cleans itself up, and use -i deliberately when it matters.

Links

$ ln -s /var/log/nginx/access.log access.log   # symbolic link (a pointer by path)
$ ls -l access.log
lrwxr-xr-x  1 dave  staff  29 Aug 14 09:20 access.log -> /var/log/nginx/access.log
$ ln data.csv data-hard.csv                    # hard link (a second name for the same data)

A symlink points at a path; if the target moves, the link breaks. A hard link is a second directory entry for the same underlying data, so the data survives until every name is removed. In practice you will use symlinks ninety-nine times out of a hundred — for pointing current at release-2026-08-14, for instance.

Batch operations

$ cp *.txt backup/                     # everything matching, into a directory
$ mv report_*.pdf 2026/                # tidy by pattern
$ for f in *.jpeg; do mv "$f" "${f%.jpeg}.jpg"; done   # rename extensions in bulk

That last one uses a loop and parameter expansion — both covered in Chapter 11. It reads as: for each file ending in .jpeg, move it to the same name with the .jpeg suffix stripped and .jpg appended. Note the quotes around "$f": without them, a filename with a space breaks the command.

Lab 3 · File surgery

Work inside ~/shell-lab.

  1. Create a directory staging with subdirectories in, out, and err in a single command.
  2. Copy every .csv from data/ into staging/in/.
  3. Rename staging/in/sales_2026.csv to staging/in/sales_2026_backup.csv.
  4. Make a full recursive copy of data/ called data_snapshot/, preserving timestamps.
  5. Create a symlink called latest-log that points at logs/app.log. Confirm with ls -l that it is a link.
  6. Delete staging/err using a command that would refuse if the directory were not empty.
  7. List (do not delete) every file in data_snapshot/ that ends in .tmp, then delete them.

Questions

Why does mkdir -p matter in scripts?

Without -p, mkdir fails with a non-zero exit code if the directory already exists, which will abort a script running under set -e. With -p it succeeds silently whether or not the directory is there, and creates any missing parent directories. That property — same result no matter how many times you run it — is called idempotence and is the backbone of reliable automation.

What is actually different between cp -r and cp -a?

-r copies the tree but the copies get fresh timestamps and your ownership/umask. -a ("archive") is -r plus preservation of modification times, permissions, ownership, and symlinks (copying links as links rather than following them). Use -a for backups and deployments; -r is fine for scratch copies.

You run rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/* and BUILD_DIR was never set. What happens, and how do you prevent it?

The variable expands to nothing, so the command becomes rm -rf /* — it tries to delete everything on the system it has permission to touch. Prevention, in order of usefulness: set -u at the top of every script (unset variables become an error), always quote ("$BUILD_DIR"), and use ${BUILD_DIR:?BUILD_DIR is required} which aborts with a message if the variable is empty or unset.

Your symlink shows in red in ls output. Why?

It is broken — the path it points to no longer exists. Symlinks store a path, not a reference to the data, so moving or deleting the target leaves the link dangling. ls -l still shows you where it was pointing, and readlink -f link resolves it.

Why is moving a large file within one disk instant, but copying it slow?

mv within a single filesystem only updates directory entries — the file's data never moves. Across filesystems (say from your disk to a USB stick), mv has no such shortcut: it copies the data and then deletes the original, so it takes as long as cp.

Chapter 4Looking Inside Files

Almost everything on a Linux system is a text file: configuration, logs, data, scripts. Knowing four or five ways to read them — and which one fits the situation — removes any need to open a GUI editor to glance at something.

Reading whole files

$ cat notes.txt              # dump the whole file to the screen
$ cat -n script.sh           # with line numbers
$ cat a.txt b.txt > both.txt # concatenate — this is what "cat" is short for
$ less /var/log/syslog       # page through it interactively

Use cat for short files and less for anything you cannot see in one screen. less does not load the whole file into memory, so it opens a 4 GB log instantly.

In lessDoes
Space / bpage down / page up
g / Gjump to start / end of file
/wordsearch forward; n next match, N previous
&wordshow only lines matching — a hidden gem for logs
Ffollow the file as it grows, like tail -f; Ctrl-C to stop
qquit

Reading parts of files

$ head data.csv              # first 10 lines
$ head -n 3 data.csv         # first 3
$ tail -n 50 app.log         # last 50
$ tail -f app.log            # keep printing new lines as they arrive
$ tail -F app.log            # same, but survive log rotation
$ head -n 20 file | tail -n 5    # lines 16-20

tail -f is how you watch a service while you poke at it. Leave it running in one terminal, do the thing in another. Combine it with grep to watch only what matters:

$ tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR

Counting and measuring

$ wc -l access.log        # how many lines
128473 access.log
$ wc -w essay.txt         # words
$ wc -c image.png         # bytes
$ file mystery            # what kind of file is this, really?
mystery: PNG image data, 1200 x 800, 8-bit/color RGBA
$ stat notes.txt          # size, timestamps, permissions, inode

file looks at the content, not the extension — useful when someone hands you data.txt that is actually a gzip archive.

Comparing

$ diff old.conf new.conf         # line-by-line differences
$ diff -u old.conf new.conf      # unified format — the same format git uses
$ diff -r dir1/ dir2/            # compare whole trees
$ cmp a.bin b.bin                # byte comparison, for binaries
$ md5sum file                    # fingerprint, to check two copies match
$ diff -u old.conf new.conf
--- old.conf
+++ new.conf
@@ -3,5 +3,5 @@
 listen 80;
-worker_processes 2;
+worker_processes 4;
 keepalive_timeout 65;

Lines with - are in the first file, + in the second, and unmarked lines are context. Once you can read a unified diff you can read every code review you will ever be sent.

When it is not text

$ strings binary_file | less      # pull out the readable text
$ xxd file | head                 # hex dump
$ zcat archive.gz | less          # read a gzipped file without unpacking it
$ zgrep ERROR app.log.2.gz        # grep inside a gzipped file
Tip

Never cat a binary file. It will send control characters to your terminal and leave the display garbled. If you do, reset fixes it.

Questions

Why prefer less over cat for a large log?

cat writes the entire file to your terminal, which scrolls almost all of it past you and can take a long time for a multi-gigabyte file. less reads only the part it is displaying, so it opens instantly regardless of size, and it gives you search and navigation. The only real reason to cat a big file is to pipe it somewhere else — and even then you usually do not need cat at all (see the next question).

What is wrong with cat file.txt | grep ERROR?

Nothing breaks, but it starts an extra process for no reason — grep can open the file itself: grep ERROR file.txt. This is common enough to have a name, the "useless use of cat". It is a small thing, but on a loop over 10,000 files it stops being small.

What is the difference between tail -f and tail -F?

-f follows the open file descriptor. If logrotate renames app.log to app.log.1 and creates a fresh app.log, -f keeps watching the old, now-renamed file and goes silent. -F follows the name, so it notices the rotation and reattaches. On a long-running watch, use -F.

How do you print lines 100-110 of a file?

head -n 110 file | tail -n 11 is the portable answer and the one most people reach for. sed -n '100,110p' file is more direct and stops reading early if you add -n '100,110p;110q'. Both are fine; the head/tail version is easier to remember under pressure.

A colleague sends you config.txt and your editor shows gibberish. What do you run first?

file config.txt. Extensions on Linux are decoration; file inspects the actual bytes and will tell you it is a gzip archive, a JPEG, or UTF-16 text. Then act accordingly — zcat, an image viewer, or iconv.

Chapter 5Pipes and Redirection

This is the chapter that turns a pile of commands into a toolkit. If you only properly learn one chapter, make it this one.

Every command has three streams

When a program runs, the shell hands it three channels:

StreamNumberDefault
stdin — input0your keyboard
stdout — normal output1your screen
stderr — error output2your screen

Errors go to a separate channel on purpose, so that when you redirect output to a file the errors still reach you instead of silently landing in the data.

Redirection: pointing a stream at a file

$ ls > files.txt            # stdout to a file, overwriting it
$ ls >> files.txt           # stdout appended to the file
$ ls /nope 2> errors.txt    # stderr to a file
$ ls /nope > out.txt 2>&1   # stdout to file, then stderr to wherever stdout goes
$ ls /nope &> all.txt       # bash shorthand for the same thing
$ command > /dev/null 2>&1  # discard everything; /dev/null is the bit bucket
$ sort < unsorted.txt       # feed a file in as stdin
Order matters

2>&1 > file is not the same as > file 2>&1. Read it right to left as a series of assignments: the first sends stderr to the current stdout (the terminal) and only then moves stdout to the file — so errors still hit your screen. Put the redirection first: > file 2>&1. Or just use &>.

Pipes: one command's output as the next one's input

The | character connects stdout of the left-hand command to stdin of the right-hand one. No temporary files, and both commands run at the same time.

$ ls -l | wc -l                      # how many entries in this directory
$ ps aux | grep nginx                 # find nginx processes
$ cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l   # how many 404s (and one useless cat)
$ grep 404 access.log | wc -l         # better

A realistic pipeline reads like a sentence. This one answers "which IP addresses hit us most?":

$ cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10
  4821 10.0.0.14
  3390 10.0.0.7
   902 192.168.1.55

Step by step: take field 1 using space as the delimiter → sort so identical lines are adjacent → uniq -c collapses runs and prefixes a count → sort numerically, largest first → take the top ten. The sort | uniq -c | sort -rn sequence is such a common idiom that it is worth memorizing as a single unit.

Build pipelines one stage at a time

Do not write the whole thing and then debug it. Run cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | head, look at the output, then add | sort | uniq -c | head, look again. Adding | head at the end of an in-progress pipeline keeps the output readable while you work.

tee: a pipe with a tap

$ make 2>&1 | tee build.log            # watch the output AND save it
$ make 2>&1 | tee -a build.log         # append instead of overwrite
$ echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward=1" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

That last line solves a problem that trips up everyone: sudo echo x > /etc/file fails, because the redirection is performed by your shell (unprivileged) before sudo ever runs. tee is the program doing the writing, so sudo tee works.

xargs: turn input into arguments

Some commands read stdin (grep, sort, wc). Others only take arguments (rm, cp, mkdir). xargs bridges the two.

$ find . -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm            # delete every .tmp file
$ find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm # safe with spaces in names
$ cat servers.txt | xargs -I{} ssh {} uptime # run a command per line
$ ls *.csv | xargs -n1 wc -l                 # one argument per invocation
$ find . -name '*.jpg' | xargs -P4 -I{} convert {} {}.png   # 4 in parallel

-print0/-0 pairs null bytes as separators instead of whitespace, which is the correct way to handle filenames containing spaces. Use it by default when piping find into xargs.

Chaining on success and failure

$ mkdir build && cd build      # run the second only if the first succeeded
$ ping -c1 host || echo "host is down"   # run the second only if the first failed
$ cd /tmp ; ls                  # run both regardless

Every command returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means failure. $? holds the last one.

$ grep -q ERROR app.log
$ echo $?
0                                # 0 = found it = success

&& is the single most valuable operator in this list. cd /some/dir && rm -rf * is dramatically safer than cd /some/dir; rm -rf *, because if the cd fails, the second version deletes the contents of whatever directory you happened to be in.

Command substitution

$ echo "Today is $(date +%F)"
Today is 2026-08-14
$ tar -czf "backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz" data/
$ kill $(pgrep -f myapp)
$ files=$(ls *.txt | wc -l)

$(...) runs the command inside and substitutes its output. You may also see backticks — `date` — in older scripts; they work but do not nest, so prefer $( ).

Lab 5 · Plumbing

Work inside ~/shell-lab.

  1. Count how many lines in logs/app.log contain ERROR, using a pipe.
  2. Write the names of all files in data/ into a file called manifest.txt, then append the current date to the end of that file.
  3. Run ls /does/not/exist so that the error message goes into err.txt and nothing appears on your screen.
  4. Produce a top-5 list of the most frequent log levels in logs/app.log (the second field of each line). Expect a cut | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head pipeline.
  5. Run wc -l on logs/app.log, showing the result on screen and saving it to count.txt, in one command.
  6. Use find and xargs to delete every .tmp file under data/, handling spaces in names safely.
  7. Write a one-liner that creates a directory named after today's date and moves manifest.txt into it — and does not move anything if the directory could not be created.

Questions

Why does sudo echo "text" >> /etc/hosts fail with "permission denied"?

Because your shell sets up the >> redirection before it runs sudo, and your shell is not root. The sudo only elevates echo, which is not the process opening the file. Fix it with echo "text" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts, or sudo sh -c 'echo "text" >> /etc/hosts'.

What does 2>&1 mean, character by character?

2 is stderr, > is redirect, &1 means "to wherever file descriptor 1 currently points" — the ampersand distinguishes it from a file literally named 1. So: "send stderr to the same place stdout is going right now." Because it copies the current destination, position in the command line matters.

You want the ten largest files in a directory tree. Sketch the pipeline.

du -ah . | sort -rh | head -n 10. du -ah prints sizes for all files, sort -rh sorts human-readable sizes (so 2G beats 900M) in reverse, head trims. The -h flag on sort is the piece most people do not know about, and it is what makes this work.

When do you need xargs instead of a plain pipe?

When the receiving command reads its inputs from the command line rather than from stdin. rm, mkdir, cp, and echo ignore stdin entirely — ls | rm does nothing useful. xargs reads stdin and rebuilds it into arguments. Commands like grep, sort, wc, and sed read stdin natively, so no xargs needed.

What is the difference between cmd1 && cmd2 and cmd1 ; cmd2?

; runs cmd2 unconditionally. && runs it only if cmd1 exited 0. In anything that touches files, prefer &&: it makes the second command's precondition explicit, and it is the difference between a failed cd being harmless and being catastrophic.

How would you check whether a string appears in a file without printing anything?

grep -q PATTERN file. The -q flag suppresses output and exits as soon as it finds a match; you read the result from the exit code. That makes it the right thing to put inside an if: if grep -q ERROR app.log; then ... ; fi.

Chapter 6Finding Things

Two questions come up constantly: where is that file? and which file contains that text? The answers are find and grep.

find: locating files by their properties

find has an unusual syntax — find WHERE CONDITIONS ACTION — but you only need a handful of conditions.

$ find . -name "*.log"              # by name, case-sensitive, from here down
$ find . -iname "readme*"           # case-insensitive
$ find /etc -type f                 # files only (-type d for directories, l for links)
$ find . -size +100M                # bigger than 100 MB (+/- for more/less)
$ find . -mtime -7                  # modified in the last 7 days
$ find . -mtime +30                 # modified more than 30 days ago
$ find . -mmin -15                  # modified in the last 15 minutes
$ find . -user dave                 # owned by a user
$ find . -perm -u+x                 # executable by its owner
$ find . -maxdepth 2 -name "*.conf" # don't recurse forever

Combine conditions — they are ANDed by default:

$ find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" -size +10M -mtime +7
$ find . -name "*.tmp" -o -name "*.bak"     # -o is OR
$ find . -type f ! -name "*.md"             # ! negates

Doing something with what you found

$ find . -name "*.tmp" -delete
$ find . -name "*.log" -exec gzip {} \;      # run gzip once per file
$ find . -name "*.log" -exec rm {} +         # batch them into fewer invocations
$ find . -name "*.conf" -exec grep -l listen {} +
$ find . -name "*.sh" -print0 | xargs -0 chmod +x

{} is a placeholder for each filename. \; ends the command and runs it once per file; + packs as many filenames as fit into each invocation and is much faster on large sets.

Always look before you delete

Run the find without -delete first and read the list. find . -name "*.log " -delete — note the trailing space inside the quotes — matches nothing, but a typo the other direction can match far more than you intended.

Faster alternatives

$ locate nginx.conf        # instant, from a nightly-updated database
$ sudo updatedb            # refresh that database
$ which python3            # where is the executable I would run?
/usr/bin/python3
$ type -a python3          # every match, including aliases and functions
$ command -v docker        # the script-friendly version of `which`

locate is fast because it does not search the disk — it queries an index. That also means it will not know about a file you created five minutes ago.

grep: finding text inside files

$ grep ERROR app.log                 # lines containing ERROR
$ grep -i error app.log              # case-insensitive
$ grep -n ERROR app.log              # with line numbers
$ grep -r TODO src/                  # recursive through a directory
$ grep -c ERROR app.log              # just the count
$ grep -v DEBUG app.log              # invert: lines NOT matching
$ grep -l ERROR *.log                # just list which files matched
$ grep -w cat notes.txt              # whole word only, so "category" won't match
$ grep -A3 -B1 ERROR app.log         # 3 lines after, 1 before each match
$ grep -C2 ERROR app.log             # 2 lines of context on both sides

These flags are the whole 80%. -r, -i, -n, -v, and -C will cover almost everything you do.

$ grep -rn "TODO" --include="*.py" .        # only search Python files
$ grep -rn "password" --exclude-dir=.git .  # skip the git directory

Combining find and grep

$ find . -name "*.conf" | xargs grep -l "ssl"          # which configs mention ssl
$ find /var/log -mtime -1 -type f -exec grep -H "OOM" {} +   # yesterday's logs
$ grep -rn "deprecated" $(find . -name "*.js" -mtime -30)

Rule of thumb: use find when the file's properties matter (name, age, size, permissions), grep -r when only the content matters, and combine them when both do.

Worth installing

ripgrep (rg) is a drop-in grep -r replacement that is dramatically faster, respects .gitignore automatically, and needs no flags for the common case: rg TODO. Nothing in this book depends on it, but if you search code daily it is the single best quality-of-life install.

Lab 6 · Search and rescue

Work inside ~/shell-lab.

  1. Find every file under ~/shell-lab whose name ends in .log.
  2. Find every file modified in the last day, at most two directories deep.
  3. Find all directories named tmp anywhere in the sandbox.
  4. List every file larger than 1 KB in data/.
  5. Show every line in logs/app.log containing ERROR, with line numbers and two lines of surrounding context.
  6. Count how many lines in logs/app.log are not DEBUG.
  7. Search recursively for the word timeout in conf/, printing only the filenames that contain it.
  8. Find every .sh file in the sandbox and make it executable, safely handling spaces in filenames.

Questions

When would you use locate over find?

When you want a file by name, anywhere on the system, right now, and it has existed since at least last night. locate reads a prebuilt index so it returns instantly; find / walks the entire disk and can take minutes. Use find when you need current results or when you are filtering on size, age, ownership, or permissions — things the index does not track.

What is the difference between -exec cmd {} \; and -exec cmd {} +?

\; runs the command once per file — 5,000 files means 5,000 processes. + appends as many filenames as will fit onto a single command line, so the same job might take three invocations. Use + whenever the command accepts multiple files (most do). Use \; when the command takes exactly one file, or when you need {} to appear more than once.

grep -r ERROR . in a git repo is slow and full of noise. Two ways to fix it?

Either narrow it — grep -rn ERROR --include="*.py" --exclude-dir=.git . — or use rg ERROR, which skips .git and anything in .gitignore by default and is parallelized. For a one-off, the flags are fine; if you do this daily, install ripgrep.

How do you find files modified in the last 30 minutes?

find . -mmin -30. Note that -mtime counts in days and -mmin in minutes, and that the minus sign means "less than" (i.e. more recent). -mtime +30 means older than 30 days; -mtime -30 means within the last 30 days. Getting the sign backwards is the classic mistake.

You need every line that mentions "error" in any case, but not lines that also say "ignorable". How?

Chain two greps: grep -i error app.log | grep -v ignorable. Piping greps together is the normal way to build up include/exclude logic, and it is far more readable than trying to express the whole thing as one regex.

Chapter 7grep, sed, and awk

Three tools handle nearly all text manipulation: grep selects lines, sed edits lines, awk works with fields. Around them sits a supporting cast — sort, uniq, cut, tr — that does the simple jobs. You do not need to master any of these. You need a working subset, which is what follows.

Regular expressions, the 20% of them

All three tools speak regex. Here is the part that matters:

PatternMatches
.any single character
*zero or more of the previous thing
+one or more (needs grep -E)
?zero or one (needs grep -E)
^start of line
$end of line
[abc]any one of a, b, c
[^abc]any character except a, b, c
[0-9]any digit
\.a literal dot (backslash escapes)
a|ba or b (needs grep -E)
(ab)+grouping (needs grep -E)
{2,4}between 2 and 4 repetitions

Use grep -E (extended regex) so that +, ?, |, and () work without backslashes. Use grep -F when you want no regex at all — searching for a literal string containing dots or slashes.

$ grep -E '^ERROR' app.log                    # lines starting with ERROR
$ grep -E 'error|fail|panic' app.log          # any of three words
$ grep -E '[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}' contacts.txt    # a phone-shaped pattern
$ grep -E '^\s*$' file.txt                    # blank lines
$ grep -F '192.168.1.1' access.log            # literal, dots are just dots
Always single-quote your patterns

grep '$USER' file searches for the literal text $USER; grep "$USER" file searches for your username. Regex is full of characters bash also wants to interpret ($ * ? [ ] \), so single quotes are the default and double quotes are the deliberate exception.

sed: search and replace on a stream

Ninety percent of real sed use is one command, s for substitute:

$ sed 's/old/new/' file.txt          # first occurrence on each line
$ sed 's/old/new/g' file.txt         # every occurrence (g = global)
$ sed 's/old/new/gi' file.txt        # global, case-insensitive
$ sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt      # edit the file in place
$ sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file.txt  # in place, keeping file.txt.bak

The delimiter does not have to be /. When your text contains slashes, switch it:

$ sed 's|/usr/local/bin|/opt/bin|g' paths.conf

The other handful of sed features worth knowing:

$ sed -n '5p' file.txt              # print only line 5 (-n suppresses default printing)
$ sed -n '10,20p' file.txt          # lines 10 through 20
$ sed '/^#/d' config.conf           # delete comment lines
$ sed '/^$/d' file.txt              # delete blank lines
$ sed 's/^[ \t]*//' file.txt        # strip leading whitespace
$ sed '2i\inserted line' file.txt   # insert before line 2
$ sed 's/\(.*\):\(.*\)/\2:\1/' pairs.txt   # swap around a colon using groups

In the last example \( \) captures a group and \1, \2 refer back to them in the replacement. With sed -E you can drop the backslashes: sed -E 's/(.*):(.*)/\2:\1/'.

On macOS

macOS ships BSD sed, where -i requires an argument: sed -i '' 's/a/b/' file. GNU sed (Linux) treats -i '' as an error. If you write scripts for both, sed -i.bak works on both and leaves a backup you can delete.

awk: columns and arithmetic

awk splits each line into fields and lets you work with them. $1 is the first field, $2 the second, $0 the whole line, NF the number of fields, NR the current line number.

$ awk '{print $1}' access.log              # first column
$ awk '{print $1, $NF}' access.log         # first and last column
$ awk -F, '{print $3}' data.csv            # comma as the separator
$ awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd         # all usernames
$ awk 'NR > 1 {print $2}' data.csv         # skip the header row

Add a condition before the braces and awk becomes a filter with arithmetic:

$ awk '$3 > 100' data.txt                     # lines where field 3 exceeds 100
$ awk -F, '$2 == "ERROR" {print $1}' log.csv  # field 2 matches exactly
$ awk '/timeout/ {print NR": "$0}' app.log    # regex match, printing line numbers
$ awk 'length($0) > 80' file.txt              # lines longer than 80 characters

And the thing awk does that nothing else does as cleanly — summing a column:

$ awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum}' sales.txt
48211
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 {sum += $4; n++} END {printf "avg: %.2f\n", sum/n}' data.csv
avg: 132.47
$ awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (ip in count) print count[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn

BEGIN { } runs before the first line, END { } after the last. That last example builds a frequency table in an associative array — it is the awk version of sort | uniq -c, and it is faster because it does not sort.

sort, uniq, cut, tr

$ sort names.txt                # alphabetical
$ sort -n numbers.txt           # numeric
$ sort -rn numbers.txt          # numeric, descending
$ sort -h sizes.txt             # human sizes: 2K < 1M < 3G
$ sort -u names.txt             # sorted, duplicates removed
$ sort -t, -k3 -n data.csv      # by 3rd comma-separated field, numerically
$ sort -k2,2 -k1,1 file.txt     # by field 2, then field 1

$ uniq file.txt                 # collapse ADJACENT duplicates — sort first!
$ uniq -c file.txt              # prefix each line with its count
$ uniq -d file.txt              # only lines that were duplicated
$ uniq -u file.txt              # only lines that appeared once

$ cut -d, -f2 data.csv          # field 2, comma-delimited
$ cut -d, -f1,3 data.csv        # fields 1 and 3
$ cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd       # usernames
$ cut -c1-10 file.txt           # characters 1 through 10

$ tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < file.txt     # uppercase
$ tr -d '\r' < dos.txt > unix.txt   # strip carriage returns
$ tr -s ' ' < file.txt          # squeeze runs of spaces into one
$ tr ' ' '\n' < file.txt        # one word per line
The rule that trips everyone

uniq only removes adjacent duplicate lines. It is a streaming tool with no memory. Always sort first: sort file | uniq -c. If you forget, you get a wrong answer rather than an error, which is worse.

Choosing between them

JobReach for
Which lines contain X?grep
Replace X with Y everywheresed
Pull out column 3cut if the delimiter is consistent, awk if not
Sum or average a columnawk
Count occurrencessort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Anything involving JSONjq, not these
More than ~20 lines of awkPython
Lab 7 · Text wrangling

Work inside ~/shell-lab. data/sales_2026.csv has a header row and columns: date,region,product,units,revenue.

  1. Print just the region column, skipping the header.
  2. List each region once, with a count of how many rows it has, sorted most-frequent first.
  3. Sum the revenue column.
  4. Print only the rows where units is greater than 50.
  5. Compute the average revenue per row, printed to two decimal places.
  6. In conf/nginx.conf, replace every occurrence of worker_processes 2 with worker_processes 4, saving a .bak of the original.
  7. Print conf/nginx.conf with all comment lines and blank lines removed.
  8. From logs/app.log, produce a count of each log level, sorted by frequency.
  9. Convert data/names.txt to all uppercase, one word per line.

Questions

Why must you sort before uniq?

uniq compares each line only to the one immediately before it — it holds no state beyond that, which is what lets it stream a file of any size. Duplicates scattered through the file therefore survive. sort brings identical lines together first. (sort -u does both in one step, but does not give you counts, so sort | uniq -c stays useful.)

When is cut the wrong tool and awk the right one?

When fields are separated by runs of whitespace of varying width — the output of ls -l, ps, or df. cut -d' ' treats every single space as a delimiter, so a double space produces an empty field and the columns shift. awk's default splitting collapses runs of whitespace, so awk '{print $5}' just works. Use cut for clean single-character delimiters like CSV or /etc/passwd.

How would you replace a string across every .conf file in a tree?

find . -name "*.conf" -exec sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' {} +. Two safety notes: run it first without -i to see the substitutions printed, and the .bak suffix means every file gets a backup you can restore from — and then have to clean up with find . -name "*.bak" -delete.

What does awk 'NR > 1' do, and why is it so common?

NR is the current record (line) number, and a bare condition with no action block means "print the line". So NR > 1 prints everything except line 1 — it skips the header row of a CSV. The companion idiom is NR == 1 to print only the header.

Your regex grep '192.168.1.1' matches lines you did not expect. Why?

. in a regex matches any character, so that pattern also matches 192a168b1c1 and, more realistically, 192.168.1.100 as a substring. Either escape the dots (grep '192\.168\.1\.1'), anchor it with -w, or use grep -F to turn regex off entirely.

What is the awk equivalent of sort | uniq -c, and when is it better?

awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}'. It is better on very large inputs, because it makes one pass and holds only the distinct keys in memory, whereas sort must order every line. The tradeoff is that the output is unordered, so you usually append | sort -rn anyway — on a modest file, the simpler sort | uniq -c is the better choice for readability.

Chapter 8Permissions and Ownership

Every file has an owner, a group, and nine permission bits. Once the notation clicks, this stops being mysterious.

Reading the bits

-rwxr-xr--  1 dave  developers  4096 Aug 14 09:03 deploy.sh
 └─┬─┘└┬┘└┬┘    └─┬─┘  └───┬────┘
   │   │  │       │        └ group
   │   │  │       └ owner
   │   │  └ others: r-- (read only)
   │   └ group:   r-x (read, execute)
   └ owner:       rwx (read, write, execute)
BitOn a fileOn a directory
r (4)read its contentslist its contents
w (2)modify itcreate/delete files inside it
x (1)run it as a programenter it (cd) and access files inside

The directory column is the part people get wrong. You can delete a file you have no write permission on, provided you can write to the directory containing it — the permission that matters is on the directory entry, not the file. And a directory with r but no x lets you see names but not read anything inside.

chmod: changing permissions

Two notations, both worth knowing. Symbolic is readable and relative:

$ chmod +x script.sh          # make executable (for everyone, subject to umask)
$ chmod u+x script.sh         # executable by the owner only
$ chmod g-w file.txt          # remove write from the group
$ chmod o-rwx secret.txt      # others get nothing
$ chmod a+r public.txt        # everyone can read
$ chmod u=rw,go=r file.txt    # set exactly, don't add or subtract

Numeric is terse and absolute. Add the values: r=4, w=2, x=1.

NumberMeansTypical use
644rw-r--r--ordinary file: owner edits, everyone reads
755rwxr-xr-xscript or directory: everyone can run/enter
600rw-------private file: keys, credentials
700rwx------private directory
664rw-rw-r--shared with your group
777rwxrwxrwxalmost always a mistake
$ chmod 644 notes.txt
$ chmod 755 deploy.sh
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      # ssh refuses to use a key with looser permissions
$ chmod -R 755 public_html/         # recursive
Two things to avoid

chmod 777 means anyone on the system can modify the file. It is almost never the actual fix for a permission problem; it is a way of not diagnosing one. And chmod -R 755 on a tree containing files will mark every data file executable — use find . -type d -exec chmod 755 {} + and find . -type f -exec chmod 644 {} + to treat directories and files differently.

chown: changing owner and group

$ sudo chown dave file.txt              # change owner
$ sudo chown dave:developers file.txt   # change owner and group
$ sudo chown :developers file.txt       # change group only
$ sudo chgrp developers file.txt        # same thing
$ sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/

Only root can give a file away to another user, which is why chown almost always needs sudo.

Who am I, really

$ whoami
dave
$ id
uid=1000(dave) gid=1000(dave) groups=1000(dave),27(sudo),999(docker)
$ groups
dave sudo docker

Group membership is evaluated at login. If someone adds you to a group, you will not have it until you log out and back in — a frequent source of "but I am in the docker group" confusion.

sudo

$ sudo systemctl restart nginx      # run one command as root
$ sudo -i                            # start an interactive root shell
$ sudo -u postgres psql              # run as some other user
$ sudo !!                            # rerun your last command with sudo

That last one is a history expansion — !! means "the previous command line" — and it is the single most-used trick in this book once you know it.

Prefer sudo cmd over sudo -i

A root shell has no seatbelt and no record of what you did in it. Running individual commands with sudo keeps each one logged and keeps your default state unprivileged, so a mistyped rm is merely annoying instead of fatal.

umask: default permissions

$ umask
0022
$ touch new.txt && ls -l new.txt
-rw-r--r--  1 dave  staff  0 Aug 14 09:30 new.txt

umask subtracts from the maximum default (666 for files, 777 for directories). With umask 022: 666 − 022 = 644 for a new file, 755 for a new directory. That is why new files are never executable by default — a sensible safety property.

Lab 8 · Locking things down

Work inside ~/shell-lab.

  1. Show the permissions of everything in scripts/ in long format.
  2. Make scripts/backup.sh executable by its owner only, then run it with ./scripts/backup.sh.
  3. Set conf/secrets.env so only its owner can read or write it. Verify with ls -l.
  4. Express rw-r----- in numeric notation, then apply it to data/sales_2026.csv.
  5. Create a directory private/ that nobody but you can enter.
  6. Using find, set every directory under data/ to 755 and every file to 644, in two commands.
  7. Print your user id, group id, and every group you belong to.
  8. What is your current umask? Create a file and confirm the permissions match what the umask predicts.

Questions

Translate chmod 750 into words.

Owner 7 = 4+2+1 = read, write, execute. Group 5 = 4+1 = read and execute, no write. Others 0 = nothing at all. So: rwxr-x---. A common setting for a script that a team runs but outsiders should not even see the contents of.

You have read permission on a file but cannot open it. What is likely wrong?

You lack execute (x) permission on one of the directories in its path. To reach /a/b/c/file you need x on /a, /a/b, and /a/b/c — execute on a directory means "may traverse". Check with namei -l /a/b/c/file, which shows the permissions at every level of the path.

Why can you delete a file you do not own and have no write permission on?

Deleting removes a name from a directory, so the permission checked is w on the containing directory, not on the file. This is why /tmp has the "sticky bit" (drwxrwxrwt — note the t): it is world-writable, but the sticky bit restricts deletion to the file's owner. Without it, anyone could clear out everyone else's temp files.

Your script fails with "permission denied" even though you can read it. Two possible causes?

Either the file is not executable (chmod +x script.sh), or the filesystem it lives on is mounted noexec — common for /tmp on hardened systems. A third, sneakier cause: the shebang line points at an interpreter that does not exist, which some shells report as a confusingly similar error. As a workaround you can always run bash script.sh, which does not require the execute bit.

Why does ssh refuse your private key?

Because its permissions are too open. SSH requires the private key be readable only by you — chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 — and the ~/.ssh directory be 700. It refuses rather than warns, on the reasoning that a key other users can read is already compromised.

Chapter 9Processes and Jobs

A process is a running program. The shell gives you tools to see them, control the ones you started, and stop the ones you did not.

Seeing what is running

$ ps aux                       # every process on the system
$ ps aux | grep nginx          # the ones you care about
$ ps -ef                       # the same information, different formatting
$ pgrep -a nginx               # PIDs and command lines, without the grep noise
$ top                          # live, sorted by CPU
$ htop                         # top, but pleasant (install separately)

The columns in ps aux that matter: PID (the number you need to kill it), %CPU and %MEM, STAT (R running, S sleeping, Z zombie, D uninterruptible), and COMMAND.

$ ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 6      # top 5 memory consumers
$ ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p 4821            # specific fields for one PID

In top: M sorts by memory, P by CPU, k kills a PID, q quits, 1 shows per-core CPU.

Stopping processes

$ kill 4821                # polite: SIGTERM, asks it to shut down cleanly
$ kill -9 4821             # forceful: SIGKILL, cannot be caught or ignored
$ kill -HUP 4821           # SIGHUP: many daemons reload their config on this
$ pkill nginx              # kill by name
$ pkill -f "python app.py" # match against the full command line
$ killall firefox          # kill every process with that exact name

Always try kill before kill -9. SIGTERM lets a program flush its buffers, close database connections, and remove its lock file. SIGKILL removes it from the kernel's process table mid-sentence, and the cleanup becomes your problem.

SignalNumberMeaning
SIGHUP1terminal closed; by convention, "reload your config"
SIGINT2what Ctrl-C sends
SIGKILL9die now, uncatchable
SIGTERM15please exit — the default for kill
SIGSTOP / SIGCONT19 / 18pause / resume, what Ctrl-Z and fg use

Job control: managing what you started

$ long_running_command &      # start it in the background
[1] 4821
$ jobs                         # list this shell's jobs
[1]+  Running    long_running_command &
$ fg %1                        # bring job 1 to the foreground
$ bg %1                        # resume a stopped job in the background
$ Ctrl-Z                       # suspend the foreground job
$ kill %1                      # kill by job number rather than PID

The everyday sequence: you start something, realize it will take ten minutes, press Ctrl-Z to suspend it, type bg to let it continue in the background, and get your prompt back. When it finishes, bash tells you.

Surviving a disconnect

Background jobs die when your shell exits, which matters over SSH.

$ nohup ./long_job.sh &             # ignore SIGHUP; output goes to nohup.out
$ nohup ./job.sh > job.log 2>&1 &   # ...with output where you want it
$ disown -h %1                       # detach a job you already started

For anything you will want to come back to, use a terminal multiplexer instead:

$ tmux new -s deploy      # start a named session
  (do work; press Ctrl-b then d to detach)
$ tmux ls                 # list sessions
$ tmux attach -t deploy   # reattach, from anywhere, later

tmux keeps a real terminal alive on the server. Your SSH connection dropping becomes a non-event rather than a lost deployment. If you administer remote machines, this is the highest-value thing in this chapter.

What is it doing?

$ uptime                    # load average: 1, 5, 15 minute
$ free -h                   # memory
$ df -h                     # disk space by filesystem
$ du -sh /var/log/*         # what is filling the disk
$ lsof -p 4821              # which files this process has open
$ lsof -i :8080             # which process is holding port 8080
$ ss -tulpn                 # all listening sockets and their processes
$ strace -p 4821            # every syscall it makes (loud, but decisive)

"Which process has port 8080?" is asked daily; lsof -i :8080 or ss -tulpn | grep 8080 answers it.

Load average

uptime's three numbers are the average number of processes wanting CPU over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Compare them against your core count: a load of 4.0 on a 4-core machine is fully busy, on a 16-core machine it is idle. The trend across the three numbers tells you whether things are getting better or worse.

Lab 9 · Process control
  1. List the five processes using the most memory on your machine.
  2. Start sleep 300 in the background. Confirm it appears in jobs and find its PID.
  3. Bring it to the foreground, suspend it with Ctrl-Z, then resume it in the background.
  4. Kill it using its job number, then start another and kill it by PID.
  5. Start sleep 300 in the foreground, suspend it, and confirm with ps that its state is T (stopped).
  6. Find every process whose command line contains sleep, using one command and no grep.
  7. Show your machine's load average, free memory, and disk usage.
  8. Find out which process is listening on a port — try 22 if you have sshd running.
  9. Run ./scripts/slow.sh with nohup so it survives closing the terminal, sending its output to slow.log.

Questions

Why is kill -9 a last resort?

SIGKILL is handled by the kernel and never reaches the program, so it gets no chance to run cleanup code: buffers are not flushed (data loss), temp files and lock files are left behind, child processes can be orphaned, and databases may need recovery on restart. Send SIGTERM, wait a few seconds, and only escalate if the process ignores it. A process that ignores SIGTERM repeatedly is usually stuck in uninterruptible I/O (state D), where even SIGKILL will not help until the I/O completes.

What is the difference between &, nohup, and tmux?

& backgrounds a job within your current shell — it dies when the shell exits. nohup makes it ignore the hangup signal so it survives your logout, but you cannot interact with it again. tmux keeps an entire terminal session alive on the machine, so you can detach, disconnect, reconnect from a different computer, and pick up exactly where you left off, with scrollback and multiple windows intact.

You pressed Ctrl-Z and your program stopped. Is it still running?

No — it is suspended, not running and not consuming CPU. It sits in state T holding its memory. fg resumes it in the foreground, bg resumes it in the background. Forgetting a suspended job and closing the terminal will usually kill it, which is why bash warns "there are stopped jobs" when you try to exit.

How do you find what is holding port 5432?

sudo lsof -i :5432 or sudo ss -tulpn | grep 5432. Both need root to show processes owned by other users — without sudo you will see the port is in use but not by whom, which is the confusing half-answer people usually get.

Your disk is full. What are the first two commands you run?

df -h to find which filesystem is full, then du -sh /path/* | sort -h on that filesystem to walk down toward the culprit, repeating a level at a time. One catch: if df shows full but du does not account for it, a deleted file is still held open by a running process — lsof | grep deleted finds it, and restarting that process releases the space.

Chapter 10The Environment and Quoting

Two topics that look unrelated but are the same subject: what the shell knows, and what the shell does to your text before running it.

Variables

$ name="Dave"              # no spaces around the = sign. None.
$ echo "$name"
Dave
$ echo "${name}s laptop"   # braces disambiguate where the name ends
$ unset name

A variable set this way is local to your shell. export makes it part of the environment, which means child processes inherit it:

$ export API_URL="https://api.example.com"
$ printenv API_URL
$ env | sort | less              # everything currently exported
$ API_KEY=secret ./script.sh     # set it for one command only
VariableHolds
$PATHcolon-separated directories searched for commands
$HOMEyour home directory
$USERyour username
$PWDcurrent directory
$SHELLyour login shell
$EDITORwhich editor other programs should open
$?exit code of the last command
$$PID of the current shell
$0name of the running script

PATH

$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin
$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3
$ export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"    # prepend, so your version wins

When you type python3, bash walks PATH left to right and runs the first match. This explains two everyday mysteries: "command not found" for a program you know is installed (its directory is not in PATH), and "why is it running the wrong version" (an earlier PATH entry wins).

Never put . in your PATH

If the current directory is searched for commands, then cd-ing into a directory someone else can write to and typing ls may run their ls. This is why running a script in the current directory requires the explicit ./script.sh.

Quoting: the rules that cause the most bugs

FormBehavior
'single'everything is literal. No expansion of any kind.
"double"expands $variables, $(commands), and backslashes; protects spaces and globs.
no quotesexpands everything, and splits on whitespace, and expands globs.
$ file="my report.txt"
$ ls $file          # ls sees TWO arguments: "my" and "report.txt" — fails
$ ls "$file"        # ls sees one argument — works
$ echo '$HOME'
$HOME
$ echo "$HOME"
/home/dave

The rule that will serve you for years: double-quote every variable expansion unless you have a specific reason not to. Filenames with spaces, empty variables, and values containing * all break unquoted code, and they break at the worst possible moment.

$ rm $file          # if file="" this becomes bare `rm` — harmless
$ rm -rf $dir/*     # if dir="" this becomes `rm -rf /*` — catastrophic
$ rm -rf "$dir"/*   # if dir="" this errors out safely

What bash does before running your command

Understanding the order removes most surprises. Bash processes a line roughly like this:

  1. Brace expansion — {a,b} becomes a b
  2. Tilde expansion — ~ becomes /home/dave
  3. Parameter expansion — $VAR becomes its value
  4. Command substitution — $(cmd) becomes cmd's output
  5. Word splitting — unquoted results split on whitespace
  6. Glob expansion — *.txt becomes the matching filenames
  7. Redirection is set up, then the command finally runs

Two consequences you will meet in practice. First, a variable's value is re-split and glob-expanded at step 5 and 6 — which is exactly why quoting matters. Second, redirection happens last, in your shell, which is why sudo cmd > /root/file fails (Chapter 5).

Parameter expansion tricks

$ f="report.tar.gz"
$ echo "${f%.gz}"        # strip shortest match from the END   -> report.tar
$ echo "${f%%.*}"        # strip longest match from the END    -> report
$ echo "${f#report.}"    # strip shortest from the START       -> tar.gz
$ echo "${#f}"           # length                              -> 14
$ echo "${f/tar/TAR}"    # replace first occurrence
$ echo "${name:-guest}"  # use "guest" if name is unset or empty
$ echo "${name:?must be set}"   # abort with a message if unset

These avoid spawning basename, sed, or cut for trivial string surgery, which matters inside loops.

Making it stick: .bashrc

Settings typed at the prompt vanish when you close the terminal. To make them permanent, put them in ~/.bashrc.

# ~/.bashrc

export EDITOR=vim
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"

alias ll='ls -lah'
alias ..='cd ..'
alias gs='git status'
alias grep='grep --color=auto'

# a function, for when an alias isn't enough
mkcd() { mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1"; }

# bigger history, no duplicates, appended not overwritten
HISTSIZE=50000
HISTFILESIZE=50000
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth:erasedups
shopt -s histappend
$ source ~/.bashrc      # apply without opening a new terminal
$ . ~/.bashrc           # same thing, shorter

~/.bashrc runs for every interactive non-login shell — new terminal windows. ~/.bash_profile runs for login shells (SSH sessions, console logins). The conventional fix is to have .bash_profile source .bashrc so you only maintain one file. On macOS with zsh, the equivalent file is ~/.zshrc.

History

$ history | tail -n 20
$ history | grep docker      # what was that command last week?
$ !!                          # last command
$ sudo !!                     # last command, with sudo
$ !342                        # command number 342
$ !ssh                        # most recent command starting with ssh
$ !$                          # last argument of the previous command
$ Ctrl-R                      # interactive reverse search — type a few chars

Ctrl-R is the one to build a habit around. Press it, type any fragment of a command you ran before, press Ctrl-R again to cycle further back, Enter to run or → to edit. It replaces most of what people use ↑ for.
