Questions

Why does name = "Dave" fail?

Bash splits on whitespace, so it reads name as a command and = and "Dave" as its arguments — hence "name: command not found". Assignment requires no spaces: name="Dave". This is unlike essentially every programming language, and it catches everyone once.

What is the difference between setting a variable and exporting it?

A plain assignment lives only in the current shell. export puts it in the environment, which is copied into every child process the shell spawns. So a script you run cannot see FOO=bar but can see export FOO=bar. Note that the flow is one-way: a child can never modify its parent's environment, which is why a script cannot change your working directory unless you source it.

When is it correct to leave a variable unquoted?

Rarely, and always deliberately: when you actually want word splitting — for example FLAGS="-v -x"; cmd $FLAGS to pass two separate flags. Even then, a bash array (flags=(-v -x); cmd "${flags[@]}") is the more robust construction. Inside [[ ]], bash suppresses splitting, so quoting is optional there — but quoting anyway costs nothing.

You added a directory to PATH in .bashrc but the command still is not found in your open terminal. Why?

.bashrc is read when a shell starts. Existing shells never re-read it. Run source ~/.bashrc in the open terminal, or open a new one. If it still fails, check with echo $PATH that the export actually took, and with ls -l that the target file is executable.

What does ${VAR:-default} do, and how is it different from ${VAR:?message}?

${VAR:-default} substitutes default when VAR is unset or empty, leaving VAR itself unchanged — it is how you give a script an optional argument. ${VAR:?message} instead prints the message to stderr and exits with an error when VAR is unset or empty — it is how you declare a required argument in one line. Both are worth committing to memory.

Why is rm -rf "$dir"/* safer than rm -rf $dir/*?

If $dir is empty or unset, the unquoted version collapses to rm -rf /* — the shell removes the empty word entirely, leaving a leading slash. The quoted version expands to rm -rf ""/*, which is not a valid path and fails harmlessly. Add set -u to your scripts and the unset case becomes an error before it ever reaches rm.

Chapter 11Writing Scripts

A shell script is a file containing the commands you would have typed. That is the whole concept — but a few conventions separate a script that works today from one that works in six months on someone else's machine.

Your first script

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "Hello from $0"
echo "Running as $(whoami) on $(hostname)"
$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh

Two lines of boilerplate, both worth understanding:

The shebang #!/usr/bin/env bash tells the kernel which interpreter to use. Using env finds bash wherever it lives, which matters because it is /bin/bash on Linux and often /opt/homebrew/bin/bash on a Mac. Writing #!/bin/sh instead means a stricter POSIX shell where bash-isms like [[ ]] and arrays are unavailable.

set -euo pipefail is the single highest-value line in shell scripting:

  • -e — exit immediately if any command fails, instead of ploughing ahead
  • -u — treat an unset variable as an error, instead of silently expanding to nothing
  • -o pipefail — a pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last one

Without it, cd /nonexistent; rm -rf * in a script does exactly what you fear. With it, the script stops at the cd.

Arguments

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "script name : $0"
echo "first arg   : $1"
echo "all args    : $@"
echo "how many    : $#"

if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: $0 SOURCE [DEST]" >&2
  exit 1
fi

src="$1"
dest="${2:-./backup}"      # second argument is optional

Note >&2 on the usage message: errors belong on stderr so that someone piping your script's output does not get the error text mixed into their data. And exit 1 — a non-zero exit code is how your script tells &&, CI systems, and other scripts that it failed.

Conditionals

if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
  echo "it's a regular file"
elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then
  echo "it's a directory"
else
  echo "no such thing" >&2
  exit 1
fi

Use [[ ]] in bash, not the older [ ]: it does not split unquoted variables, supports && and || inside, and supports regex matching with =~.

TestTrue when
-f FILEexists and is a regular file
-d DIRexists and is a directory
-e PATHexists, whatever it is
-r / -w / -xyou can read / write / execute it
-s FILEexists and is not empty
-z "$S"string is empty
-n "$S"string is not empty
"$a" == "$b"strings are equal
"$a" != "$b"strings differ
$a -eq $bnumbers equal (also -ne -lt -le -gt -ge)
"$s" =~ ^abstring matches the regex
String vs number comparison

== compares strings, -eq compares numbers. [[ "10" == "9" ]] is false and [[ 10 -gt 9 ]] is true, but [[ "10" > "9" ]] is false — because as strings, "1" sorts before "9". Mixing these up produces code that is right for single-digit inputs and wrong afterwards.

Any command can be a condition — the exit code is the test:

if grep -q ERROR app.log; then
  echo "errors found"
fi

if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "docker is not installed" >&2
  exit 1
fi

Loops

for f in *.txt; do
  echo "processing $f"
  mv "$f" "processed_$f"
done

for i in {1..5}; do echo "attempt $i"; done

for host in web-01 web-02 db-01; do
  ssh "$host" 'uptime'
done

# read a file line by line — note the quoting and IFS
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "line: $line"
done < servers.txt

# loop until something succeeds
until curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health >/dev/null; do
  echo "waiting for service..."
  sleep 2
done

while IFS= read -r line is the correct incantation for reading a file line by line: IFS= stops leading and trailing whitespace being stripped, and -r stops backslashes being interpreted. Memorize it as a unit.

Do not loop over ls

for f in $(ls) breaks on any filename containing a space or a glob character. for f in * is both simpler and correct, because glob expansion produces properly separated words. For recursive work, use find -print0 with while IFS= read -r -d '' f.

case

case "$1" in
  start)   echo "starting..." ;;
  stop)    echo "stopping..." ;;
  restart) echo "restarting..." ;;
  *)       echo "usage: $0 {start|stop|restart}" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

Cleaner than a chain of elif when you are matching one variable against several literal values, and it supports globs in the patterns (*.txt)).

Functions

log() {
  echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*" >&2
}

backup() {
  local src="$1"
  local dest="${2:-/backup}"
  mkdir -p "$dest"
  tar -czf "$dest/$(basename "$src")-$(date +%F).tar.gz" "$src"
}

log "starting backup"
backup /etc /backup
log "done"

Functions take arguments the same way scripts do: $1, $2, $@. Always declare variables inside functions with local — without it they are global, and a function that quietly overwrites the caller's $i is a genuinely nasty bug to track down.

Making it robust

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# clean up on exit, however we exit
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT

# require an argument
target="${1:?usage: $0 TARGET}"

# check dependencies up front
for cmd in curl jq tar; do
  command -v "$cmd" >/dev/null || { echo "missing: $cmd" >&2; exit 1; }
done

echo "working in $tmpdir on $target"

trap ... EXIT runs the cleanup whether the script finishes, fails, or is interrupted — the shell equivalent of a finally block. Combined with mktemp -d, it means your script never leaves debris behind.

Two habits worth adopting immediately

Run shellcheck yourscript.sh before you trust any script. It catches unquoted variables, useless cats, and a dozen subtle bugs, and it explains each one. And run with bash -x script.sh when debugging — it prints every command with its variables expanded, which usually makes the problem obvious in seconds.

A complete example

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# rotate-logs.sh — compress logs older than N days, delete ones older than M
#
set -euo pipefail

LOG_DIR="${1:-/var/log/myapp}"
COMPRESS_AFTER_DAYS=7
DELETE_AFTER_DAYS=90

log() { echo "[$(date +'%F %T')] $*"; }

[[ -d "$LOG_DIR" ]] || { log "no such directory: $LOG_DIR"; exit 1; }

log "rotating logs in $LOG_DIR"

compressed=$(find "$LOG_DIR" -name '*.log' -type f \
               -mtime +"$COMPRESS_AFTER_DAYS" -print | wc -l)
find "$LOG_DIR" -name '*.log' -type f -mtime +"$COMPRESS_AFTER_DAYS" \
     -exec gzip {} +

deleted=$(find "$LOG_DIR" -name '*.log.gz' -type f \
            -mtime +"$DELETE_AFTER_DAYS" -print | wc -l)
find "$LOG_DIR" -name '*.log.gz' -type f -mtime +"$DELETE_AFTER_DAYS" -delete

log "compressed $compressed, deleted $deleted"
Lab 11 · Scripting

Write these into ~/shell-lab/scripts/ and make each executable.

  1. greet.sh — takes a name as an argument and prints "Hello, NAME". If no argument is given, print a usage message to stderr and exit 1.
  2. count.sh — takes a directory, prints how many files it contains. Error out if the argument is missing or is not a directory.
  3. ext.sh — loops over every file in data/ and prints its name and extension, using parameter expansion rather than cut.
  4. levels.sh — reads logs/app.log line by line and counts how many lines contain ERROR, WARN, and INFO, printing a summary at the end.
  5. backup.sh — takes a directory, creates a timestamped .tar.gz of it in a temp directory, then copies the archive into ~/shell-lab/archive/. Use trap to clean up the temp directory.
  6. svc.sh — accepts start, stop, or status using case, printing what it would do. Anything else prints usage and exits 1.
  7. Run bash -x on one of your scripts and read the trace. Then run shellcheck on all of them and fix what it reports.

Questions

What does each letter in set -euo pipefail actually prevent?

-e prevents the script from continuing after a failed command — without it, a failed cd is followed cheerfully by the next line. -u prevents typo'd or unset variable names expanding to an empty string, which is the mechanism behind most catastrophic rm accidents. pipefail prevents false | true from reporting success, which otherwise hides failures in the middle of a pipeline. Together they turn silent wrong behavior into a loud stop.

Why #!/usr/bin/env bash rather than #!/bin/bash?

env looks bash up in PATH, so the script works on systems where bash is not at /bin/bash — macOS with Homebrew bash 5, BSDs, Nix. The tradeoff is that it uses whichever bash comes first in PATH, which in a security-sensitive context (a setuid script, a cron job with a controlled environment) may be an argument for the absolute path. For everyday scripts, env is the better default.

Why is for f in $(ls) wrong?

Command substitution output is subject to word splitting, so a file named my report.txt becomes two iterations, and a file named * gets glob-expanded into every filename in the directory. for f in * avoids both: glob expansion produces a properly delimited list regardless of what the names contain. The only wrinkle is that * stays literal if nothing matches, so guard with [[ -e "$f" ]] || continue when that matters.

What does local do and why does it matter?

It scopes a variable to the function. Without it every assignment is global, so a function using i as a loop counter will silently clobber the caller's i — and the bug shows up as wrong results rather than an error. Declare every variable in every function local unless you specifically intend to modify global state.

How do you make sure a temp directory is removed even if the script fails halfway?

tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) then trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT. The EXIT trap fires on normal exit, on set -e aborts, and on SIGINT/SIGTERM, so cleanup happens on every path out of the script. Add other signals explicitly if you need to distinguish them: trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM.

Your script works when you run it but fails from cron. Most likely cause?

The environment. Cron runs with a minimal PATH (often just /usr/bin:/bin) and does not read your .bashrc, so commands you rely on are not found and variables you assume are unset. The fixes: use absolute paths for programs, set PATH explicitly at the top of the script, and never depend on the working directory — cd to where you mean to be. Redirecting output to a log file (>> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1) is what lets you see the error at all.

Chapter 12Working Fast

The last 20% is not new commands — it is the friction between you and the ones you know. This chapter is a collection of things that each save a few seconds, several dozen times a day.

Editing the command line

Bash uses readline, which has emacs keybindings by default. These work at every bash prompt and in most REPLs (psql, python, node):

KeysDoes
Ctrl-A / Ctrl-Ejump to start / end of line
Alt-B / Alt-Fback / forward one word
Ctrl-Wdelete the word before the cursor
Ctrl-U / Ctrl-Kdelete to start / end of line
Ctrl-Ypaste back what you just deleted
Ctrl-Rreverse search through history
Ctrl-Lclear the screen
Ctrl-C / Ctrl-Dcancel this line / end of input
Alt-.insert the last argument of the previous command

Two of these carry most of the value. Ctrl-R to find any command you have run before, and Ctrl-U then Ctrl-Y to stash a half-typed command, run something else, then paste it back.

History expansion

$ sudo !!               # rerun the last command with sudo
$ !$                     # the last argument of the previous line
$ mkdir /a/long/path && cd !$      # ...becomes cd /a/long/path
$ ^typo^fixed            # rerun the last command with one substitution
$ !ssh                   # last command that started with ssh
$ !ssh:p                 # print it without running it — check before you leap

Archives and transfers

$ tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/     # create gzipped archive
$ tar -xzf archive.tar.gz          # extract
$ tar -tzf archive.tar.gz          # list contents without extracting
$ tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C /dest # extract somewhere specific

$ scp file.txt user@host:/path/    # copy to a remote machine
$ scp user@host:/path/file.txt .   # copy from one
$ rsync -avz --progress src/ user@host:/dest/   # sync, resumable, only changes
$ rsync -avz --dry-run src/ dest/  # show what WOULD happen

Remember tar's flags as a sentence: create or extract or list, z for gzip, f for "the filename follows". -f must come last because the filename is its argument.

rsync beats scp for anything nontrivial: it transfers only the differences, resumes after an interruption, and --dry-run lets you check first. The trailing slash on the source means "the contents of", and getting it wrong is the classic rsync mistake.

Network basics

$ curl -s https://api.example.com/status | jq .
$ curl -I https://example.com                  # headers only
$ curl -fsSL -o file.tar.gz https://host/f.tgz # fail loudly, follow redirects
$ curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
       -d '{"key":"value"}' https://api.example.com/items

$ ssh user@host                       # log in
$ ssh user@host 'df -h'               # run one command and come back
$ ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@host  # with a specific key
$ ssh-copy-id user@host               # install your key so you stop typing passwords

$ ss -tulpn        # listening ports
$ dig example.com +short
$ ping -c 4 example.com
$ traceroute example.com

curl -fsSL is worth memorizing as a unit: fail on HTTP errors instead of saving the error page, silent, Show errors anyway, L follow redirects.

SSH config

Put this in ~/.ssh/config and stop retyping connection details:

Host prod
    HostName 10.0.4.21
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_prod
    ServerAliveInterval 60

Host *.internal
    User admin
    ProxyJump bastion.example.com
$ ssh prod          # instead of ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_prod deploy@10.0.4.21

Tab completion works on these host names, and scp, rsync, and git all respect the file too.

Scheduling

$ crontab -e         # edit your scheduled jobs
$ crontab -l         # list them
# ┌─ minute (0-59)
# │ ┌─ hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌─ day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌─ month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌─ day of week (0-6, Sunday = 0)
# │ │ │ │ │
  0 2 * * *   /home/dave/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
  */15 * * * * /home/dave/bin/check.sh
  0 9 * * 1   /home/dave/bin/weekly-report.sh

Three rules that prevent the usual cron pain: use absolute paths for everything, redirect output to a log file (otherwise it is emailed into the void), and test the script by running it with a stripped environment first: env -i /bin/bash --noprofile --norc /path/to/script.sh.

A handful of things worth knowing exist

$ !!                      # you know this one now
$ cd -                     # previous directory
$ pushd /tmp ; popd        # a directory stack, for hopping around
$ time ./slow.sh           # how long did that take
$ watch -n2 'df -h /'      # rerun a command every 2 seconds
$ yes | some-command       # answer y to everything
$ seq 1 10                 # generate a sequence
$ shuf -n 5 lines.txt      # random sample
$ column -t -s, data.csv   # align CSV into readable columns
$ jq '.items[].name' r.json # query JSON properly
$ base64 -w0 file          # encode
$ openssl rand -hex 16     # a random token
$ df -h; free -h; uptime   # the three-command health check
The compounding habit

Every time you type a long command a second time, stop and decide: alias, function, or script? A one-liner you use daily becomes an alias. A parameterized one becomes a shell function in .bashrc. Anything longer than five lines becomes a script in ~/bin. Twenty minutes spent on this in your first month pays back for years.

Where to go from here

You now have the 20%. The natural next steps, roughly in order of payoff:

  • tmux — persistent sessions and split panes. An afternoon to learn, permanent benefit.
  • vim or nano — you will eventually need to edit a file on a machine with nothing else. Learn enough vim to open, edit, save, and quit: i to insert, Esc, :wq to write and quit, :q! to bail out.
  • ripgrep, fd, fzf, bat — modern replacements for grep, find, and cat. fzf in particular transforms Ctrl-R.
  • shellcheck — install it, run it on everything you write.
  • jq — once your pipelines start touching APIs, jq is to JSON what awk is to columns.
  • Bash Pitfalls and the Bash FAQ — the best free references for the things that will bite you.
Lab 12 · Speed run
  1. Run ls -la /etc, then rerun it with sudo using two keystrokes.
  2. Type a long path with mkdir -p, then cd into it without retyping the path.
  3. Use Ctrl-R to find and rerun a command from Lab 5.
  4. Create a gzipped tar of ~/shell-lab/data, list its contents without extracting, then extract it into a new directory.
  5. Use rsync --dry-run to preview syncing data/ into data_mirror/, then do it for real.
  6. Time how long find ~ -type f | wc -l takes.
  7. Use watch to display free disk space refreshing every two seconds. Quit it.
  8. Add an ~/.ssh/config entry (real or fictional) and confirm ssh <name> tab-completes.
  9. Write a cron entry that runs ~/shell-lab/scripts/backup.sh every day at 03:30 and logs its output.
  10. Pick the command you have typed most often this week and turn it into an alias or a function in your .bashrc.

Questions

What is the difference between scp and rsync?

scp copies everything, every time, and starts over if interrupted. rsync compares source and destination and transfers only the differences, can resume, preserves permissions and timestamps with -a, compresses in flight with -z, and offers --dry-run. For a single small file scp is fine; for a directory or anything you will repeat, use rsync.

Why does a cron job fail when the same script works from your shell?

Cron gives the job a nearly empty environment: a minimal PATH, no .bashrc, no DISPLAY, and the home directory as the working directory. Anything your interactive shell set up for you is absent. Diagnose it by capturing output — add >> /tmp/job.log 2>&1 to the crontab line — and fix it by setting PATH at the top of the script and using absolute paths throughout.

What do the flags in tar -xzf mean, and why must -f come last?

x extract, z decompress with gzip, f the archive filename follows. -f takes the next word as its argument, so anything after it is treated as the filename. tar -xfz archive.tar.gz tries to open a file literally named z.

You need to run a 6-hour job on a remote server over a flaky connection. What do you do?

SSH in, start tmux (or screen), run the job inside it, and detach with Ctrl-b d. The session keeps running on the server independently of your connection; reattach later with tmux attach. nohup job & also survives the disconnect but gives you no way to interact with the job afterwards, which matters when it prompts or when you want to watch it.

What is the single fastest way to reuse a command you ran an hour ago?

Ctrl-R, then type any distinctive fragment of it — press Ctrl-R again to step further back through matches, Enter to run, or → to load it into the line for editing. It beats pressing ↑ forty times and beats history | grep because it puts the result straight onto your command line.

Scripting skeleton

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

target="${1:?usage: $0 TARGET}"
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT

log() { echo "[$(date +'%F %T')] $*" >&2; }

if [[ -d "$target" ]]; then
  for f in "$target"/*; do
    [[ -f "$f" ]] || continue
    log "processing ${f##*/}"
  done
else
  log "not a directory: $target"
  exit 1
fi
TestTrue when
-f / -d / -e / -sis a file / a directory / exists / is non-empty
-z "$s" / -n "$s"string empty / non-empty
"$a" == "$b"strings equal
$a -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge $bnumeric comparison

Remote, archives, scheduling

CommandDoes

tar -xzf a.tgz / -tzfextract / list without extracting
ssh user@host 'cmd'run one command remotely
ssh-copy-id user@hoststop typing passwords
scp f user@host:/path/copy one file
rsync -avz --dry-run src/ dst/preview a sync; drop --dry-run to do it
curl -fsSL URLfetch, failing loudly, following redirects
crontab -e / -ledit / list scheduled jobs
cron fields: min hour day-of-month month day-of-week — always use absolute paths and redirect output

You don't need to run this in this edition

Every live sandbox on this page is already seeded with exactly the data this script produces — it runs in your browser, not on a real machine. This script is here so you can build the same sandbox on a real Linux box or WSL if you want to practice outside the browser too.

Question 9: echo '$USER' prints the literal text $USER; echo "$USER" prints your username. Single quotes suppress all expansion.

Lab 11 · Scripting

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# greet.sh
set -euo pipefail
name="${1:?usage: $0 NAME}"
echo "Hello, $name"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count.sh
set -euo pipefail
dir="${1:?usage: $0 DIRECTORY}"
[[ -d "$dir" ]] || { echo "not a directory: $dir" >&2; exit 1; }
n=$(find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f | wc -l)
echo "$dir contains $n files"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ext.sh
set -euo pipefail
for f in data/*; do
  [[ -f "$f" ]] || continue
  base="${f##*/}"                 # strip the path
  ext="${base##*.}"               # strip everything up to the last dot
  [[ "$ext" == "$base" ]] && ext="(none)"
  printf '%-24s %s\n' "$base" "$ext"
done
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# levels.sh
set -euo pipefail
declare -i err=0 warn=0 info=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  case "$line" in
    *ERROR*) err+=1 ;;
    *WARN*)  warn+=1 ;;
    *INFO*)  info+=1 ;;
  esac
done < logs/app.log
echo "ERROR=$err WARN=$warn INFO=$info"     # ERROR=4 WARN=3 INFO=9
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh
set -euo pipefail
src="${1:?usage: $0 DIRECTORY}"
[[ -d "$src" ]] || { echo "no such directory: $src" >&2; exit 1; }
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
name="$(basename "$src")-$(date +%F).tar.gz"
tar -czf "$tmp/$name" "$src"
mkdir -p "$HOME/shell-lab/archive"
cp "$tmp/$name" "$HOME/shell-lab/archive/"
echo "wrote archive/$name"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# svc.sh
set -euo pipefail
case "${1:-}" in
  start)  echo "would start the service"  ;;
  stop)   echo "would stop the service"   ;;
  status) echo "would report status"      ;;
  *)      echo "usage: $0 {start|stop|status}" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

That is the 20%. The rest is repetition — and the repetition is the point. Pick one thing from Chapter 12 and use it deliberately this week; next week pick another. Fluency at the shell is not a body of knowledge you finish acquiring, it is a set of reflexes you build a few seconds at a time.
